Jacobs Theatre — pleasures that make this production a moving, and deeply funny, living memorial to the late Stephen Sondheim."

criticReviews.author: Maya Phillips
criticReviews.excerpt: "This production either broke or mended something in me...We give nearly two hours of attention, and great theater offers us empathy and humanity in return: riches of which even the world’s wealthiest can only dream."

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: "Majok wisely doesn’t sugarcoat realities in sentimentality, but she also leaves the door ajar for an optimistic glimmer."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Majok's structure of alternating scenes struck me as schematic, with too neat a final tie-in of its two strands of plot."

criticReviews.author: Juan A. Ramirez
criticReviews.excerpt: " 'Cost of Living' is as much about struggling to make financial ends meet as it is about emotional ends, the feelings and impulses that keep us going or hold us back."

criticReviews.author: Greg Evans
criticReviews.excerpt: "As character study, 'Cost of Living' can be moving, funny and intriguing, but the plot mechanics and string-pulling undercut the drama."

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: "The actors, working under the direction of Jo Bonney, are honest and solid; Mozgala is a veritable forcefield of signals and manipulations."

criticReviews.author: Naveen Kumar
criticReviews.excerpt: "It’s the kind of trick of timing on which the play’s axis turns, and the sort of alignment of storytelling with reality that makes live theater such a thrill."

criticReviews.author: Johnny Oleksinski
criticReviews.excerpt: "In zig-zagging away from well-tread paths, Majok arrives at a destination we hadn’t planned to visit, but are pleased to be at nonetheless."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: The technical elements are top-notch, intensifying naturalism until it grazes the surreal.

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: " A last-minute harmonious quartet nearly makes for a happy ending."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "...these ten actors don’t hit a false note, and they blend together seamlessly."

criticReviews.author: Helen Shaw
criticReviews.excerpt: "Headland does sometimes overload the table with narrative."

criticReviews.author: Daniel D'Addario
criticReviews.excerpt: "There is so much good and sharp in 'Cult of Love'”

criticReviews.author: Naveen Kumar
criticReviews.excerpt: "feels more like seasonal content than captivating theater."

criticReviews.author: Shania Russell
criticReviews.excerpt: "Laugh, cry, and ponder harsh truths about family dysfunction"

criticReviews.author: Pete Hempstead
criticReviews.excerpt: In our acrimonious times, it might be better to stop talking and just turn on some music.

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "The way the book merrily hopscotches from cliché to cliché can still raise smiles. But 'Dames' ultimately founders on our familiarity, not with the genre it plays with like a cat’s toy, but with the long history, since its creation, of similar simulations of old-school entertainments. Even housed in Broadway’s smallest theater, this miniature musical, with a cast you could fit in a dinghy, seems just a little, well, at sea."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "It lands like a harmless piece of wet fluff. The first 20 minutes of wide-eyed antics are cute; then your mind starts to wander. 'Dames at Sea's' mild pastiche is passable but passé—imagine a revival, half a century from now, of a Fringe show about the ’80s—and it’s presented with tongue so far in cheek that it can’t say much at all."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "Instead of sticking close to the presentational style of Busby Berkeley spectaculars, 'Dames' literally belittled itself, making do with a cast of six and an orchestra of three on a stage barely big enough to contain Bernadette Peters. It would seem to be a category error to bring material so conceived to Broadway, and the production that just opened at the Helen Hayes, much as you root for it, fails to argue otherwise."

criticReviews.author: Terry Teachout
criticReviews.excerpt: "What’s not to like? Nothing whatsoever—but there isn’t enough to love about 'Dames at Sea,' which may have seemed sufficiently witty a half-century ago but has long since been outclassed by the encyclopedically knowing musical-comedy spoofery of 'The Drowsy Chaperone.' Compared with that big-brain homage, 'Dames' isn’t much more clever than a college show, and its parodies steer too close to their models to be other than mildly amusing."

criticReviews.author: Jeremy Gerard
criticReviews.excerpt: "‘Dames At Sea’ is a lot of fun and a tribute to the city’s inexhaustible pool of inexhaustible talent, if not actual stars…Broadway today is awash in nostalgia in the form of revivals, reboots and parodies, all done on a far larger scale and offering considerably more bang, or tap, for the buck. And good as they are, the dancers never let us forget just how hard they’re working to please us."

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: "'Dames at Sea' is a mid-1960s musical trifle that works overtime to be cheeky good fun. Thanks to a cast with twinkle-toes and polished pipes, it succeeds — for a while. Before long, though, monotony sets in and won’t go away. Even top-notch tap-dancing can get repetitive...'Dames' doesn’t make a big splash or sink. It treads water."

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "The new leading lady of 'Dames at Sea' is no Bernadette Peters. There’s nothing wrong with this revival that Peters, who played the role of Ruby in the original, couldn’t fix. But musical theater stars of her caliber don’t grow on trees, and although newcomer Eloise Kropp is a power tapper par excellence, she hasn’t the saucy charm of a Broadway Baby like Ruby — or the magnetic appeal of a star like Peters."

criticReviews.author: David Rooney
criticReviews.excerpt: "'Dames at Sea' reinvents one of those big-screen spectacles as a shrunken stage musical — a baby Busby Berkeley if you will — with an appealing cast of six that makes its featherweight pleasures infectious...A sweet candy morsel serving unapologetically empty calories."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "NYTimes Critic's Pick!...“Dana H.” is not just the story of a woman brutalized by a psychopath; it is also the story of a mother abandoned by a son. What else would a playwright do to make reparations but write a play about just that, in the process returning to her what the world had stolen: her voice."

criticReviews.author: Juan Michael Porter II
criticReviews.excerpt: "I recently reviewed a show and declared that talk business does not belong onstage. Dana H. has forced me to eat my words and to accept that there are no absolutes in theatre, particularly when the story is horrifically affecting and spectacularly executed as this show is. Dana H. should be required viewing for legal scholars, law enforcement officers, and aspirants across the country, if only to remind them that depravity reigns when they fail to do the right thing."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Five stars!...O’Connell is nothing less than astonishing...Watching Dana H. is like listening to a fascinating true-crime podcast, and part of the interest is in the mysteries that adhere to Dana’s account, which may be distorted by trauma and time."

criticReviews.author: Terry Teachout
criticReviews.excerpt: "Mr. Waters has staged it with the utmost simplicity, trusting in the force of the tale. I have never watched a more powerful piece of documentary theater: Once seen, it will stay with you for a long time to come."

criticReviews.author: Peter Marks
criticReviews.excerpt: "A mesmerizing act of electronic ventriloquism...It’s hard to say which is more absorbing: Dana’s story or O’Connell’s uncanny portrayal, requiring her to reproduce in perfect alignment with the audiotape every cough, pause, giggle and slap of the chair in which she sits for much of the 75 minutes of the piece."

criticReviews.author: Matt Windman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Given the lip-synching and lack of movement on the part of O’Connell, one may wonder why “Dana H.” needs to be a live piece of theater rather than a true crime podcast or a raw testimonial video on YouTube. But at its best, the production (directed by Les Waters, who has also staged other plays by Hnath) is compelling, terrifying, and multilayered, especially with regard to the nature of reality."

criticReviews.author: Zachary Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: "Not only is it the wildest true story on any stage in New York City, but it features a performance that must be seen to be believed."

criticReviews.author: David Finkle
criticReviews.excerpt: "A theatre piece that unmistakably demands considerable thought and even more unmistakably boasts Deirdre O’Connell’s unbounded talents."

criticReviews.author: Tim Teeman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Right now, 'Data' feels all-too present, all-too raw and indisputably somber"

criticReviews.author: Allison Considine
criticReviews.excerpt: “This moral-dilemma play contains several unexpected twists and turns, including a few that draw audible gasps from the audience.”

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: “It’s a correct if obvious idea, here rendered as didactically as if we’re watching a medieval morality play.”

criticReviews.author: Zachary Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: "Data is essential viewing for anyone who wants to understand the dystopia the AI revolution is leading to, and why it is succeeding"

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: "The debuting playwright Matthew Libby invents an all-too-plausible scenario in which the future of American democracy hangs on an algorithm's performance, putting the outcome in the hands of a callow, troubled recent college graduate. Scary enough for you?

criticReviews.author: David Finkle
criticReviews.excerpt: “With Data, Michael Libby has written an unquestionably significant play wrenched not only from today’s headlines but possibly also ripped from headlines heading our way in the frightfully near future.”

criticReviews.author: Roma Torre
criticReviews.excerpt: "Data is a serious play but there is humor, almost exclusively in the hands of Jonah who knows his limitations but compensates by taking on the persona of an over-stimulated dude. "

criticReviews.author: Victor Gluck
criticReviews.excerpt: Techno-thriller that is taken from tomorrow's headlines is one scary trip and very provocative about ICE's next step.

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: "speaks to the precise moment in which we are living to an astonishing degree.. both riveting and dispiriting"

criticReviews.author: Thom Geier
criticReviews.excerpt: Matthew Libby builds genuine suspense — and delivers several surprising twists — without resorting to clichés or trickery.

criticReviews.author: Mason Pilevsky
criticReviews.excerpt: At a time when faith and trust in our world is eroding, Data shares a startling message of hope.

criticReviews.author: Cary Wong
criticReviews.excerpt: It brings up interesting topic of conversation around lofty ideas and real-world implementation.

criticReviews.author: Elise Nussbaum
criticReviews.excerpt: Dark, unsettling, and all too plausible, Data depicts a world in which the safeguards between us and total government surveillance are flimsy indeed.

criticReviews.author: Tim Teeman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Right now, 'Data' feels all-too present, all-too raw and indisputably somber"

criticReviews.author: Allison Considine

criticReviews.author: Laura Collins-Hughes
criticReviews.excerpt: "Gone is the emotional aridity that kept the story at a strange remove."

criticReviews.author: Gillian Russo
criticReviews.excerpt: "Kelli O'Hara and Brian d'Arcy James give career-best performances"

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "If 'Days and Wine and Roses' isn’t exactly galvanizing...it is effectively sober."

criticReviews.author: Sara Holdren
criticReviews.excerpt: "...the show evokes a specific kind of quietly disheartened sigh."

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "The show...has a searing power that leaves you both stirred and shaken."

criticReviews.author: Greg Evans
criticReviews.excerpt: "despite its somber theme, Days of Wine and Roses is sumptuous from start to finish"

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: " ‘Days of Wine and Roses,’ a ‘beautifully’ executed musical"

criticReviews.author: Naveen Kumar
criticReviews.excerpt: "There are plenty of joys and sorrows to play even in a straightforward cautionary tale."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: " 'Dead Outlaw,' the feel-good musical of the season, if death and deadpan feel good to you."

criticReviews.author: Gillian Russo
criticReviews.excerpt: “Dead Outlaw...is entertainment for a paying audience, after all.”

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "That same level of commitment extends to all of Dead Outlaw. The writing is piquant and sly, the songs have verve and resonance, and every element of Cromer’s production seems to fit exactly in place."

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: "Dead Outlaw’s peculiarities are enhanced by the way it foregrounds its cast’s own idiosyncrasies."

criticReviews.author: Johnny Oleksinski
criticReviews.excerpt: "The musical has many diamonds in the rough. They’re just not polished properly by Cromer’s staging, which is awfully haphazard and diffuse for a typically sure-thing director."

criticReviews.author: Emlyn Travis
criticReviews.excerpt: "The pair are singing a much different, more raucous tune as they transform Elmer's larger-than-life story into a rollicking, country rock concert complete with a whole lot of laughs and a surprising amount of heart."

criticReviews.author: Joseph Verlezza
criticReviews.excerpt: “Andrew Durand as Elmer McCurdy has certainly turned “playing dead” into an artform.”

criticReviews.author: Thom Geier
criticReviews.excerpt: ‘Dead Outlaw’ unearths the corpse of forgotten history to an infectious rockabilly beat — elevating a twisty little yarn into a bizarro-world elegy to how the American Dream can curdle into violence, cruelty, and casual indifference.

criticReviews.author: Dominic Cavendish
criticReviews.excerpt: "The appetite for a show like this is clear but, though it’s a crowded field"

criticReviews.author: Sam Waite
criticReviews.excerpt: "In this writer’s opinion, he succeeded in these goals, and has created something which can – which should – be seen as a true theatrical achievement."

criticReviews.author: Marianka Swain
criticReviews.excerpt: “It’s our national story told with heart, humour and headers, and a beautiful celebration of an unlikely hero. Fiennes is definitely man of the match, but this is a joyful, and victorious, team effort.”

criticReviews.author: Aliya Al-Hassan
criticReviews.excerpt: " 'Dear England' is undoubtedly thoughtful, detailed, entertaining and absorbing."

criticReviews.author: Nick Curtis
criticReviews.excerpt: “This is a thrilling piece of work, popular and political as Graham always intends his plays to be, and – appropriately – a consummate team effort.”

criticReviews.author: Nick Curtis
criticReviews.excerpt: "this is a team effort, which captures the communal joy and heartache of sport"

criticReviews.author: Arifa Akbar
criticReviews.excerpt: “As endearing as it is, the production, directed by Rupert Goold, takes time to really lift off the ground, focusing on story rather than drama in the first half – and it does seem like a game of two halves.”

criticReviews.author: Andrzej Lukowski
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ‘Dear England’ is a big-hearted, technically dazzling celebration of football first and a critique of it second. If it was the other way around I wonder if it might feel a little more like a play for the ages. Graham’s best work is so improbably brilliant it carries the audacious rush of putting ten past the other team’s keeper.”

criticReviews.author: Andrzej Lukowski
criticReviews.excerpt: "A third run for Dear England is an indulgence, but it’s a well earned one."

criticReviews.author: Dominic Cavendish
criticReviews.excerpt: "State-of-the-nation playwright James Graham brilliantly captures the blokey awkwardness within our wider national story."

criticReviews.author: Dominic Cavendish
criticReviews.excerpt: "a brisk update of the decade’s biggest theatrical triumph"

criticReviews.author: Clive Davis
criticReviews.excerpt: “He shoots; he scores. James Graham’s fast-moving portrait of Gareth Southgate’s reign as the England football manager is a joyous example of populist theatre. There’s anguish, joy and a surprisingly generous helping of humour.”

criticReviews.author: Sarah Crompton
criticReviews.excerpt: "...it presents Southgate’s attempts to introduce a less divisive culture into football"

criticReviews.author: Matt Wolf
criticReviews.excerpt: “The world is indeed a mysterious thing, as this quasi-shamanistic Southgate seems somehow to intuit...The play's extraordinary achievement is to suggest that this impossibly tall order may in fact lie within reach.”

criticReviews.author: Daz Gale
criticReviews.excerpt: "A beautiful production about the beautiful game. It felt great to see a story as positive as this coming home to a London stage – I wouldn’t be surprised if this continues James Graham’s track record and gets a West End transfer itself in the not-too-distant future. If it does, it really would be very well deserved."

criticReviews.author: Mark Lawson
criticReviews.excerpt: "footballing reboot adds extra time for Gareth Southgate’s exit"

criticReviews.author: Mark Lawson
criticReviews.excerpt: "footballing reboot adds extra time for Gareth Southgate’s exit"

criticReviews.author: Demetrios Matheou
criticReviews.excerpt: "The penalty kick becomes the totem of both Southgate’s approach and the play itself"

criticReviews.author: Jessie Thompson
criticReviews.excerpt: “At almost three hours, ‘Dear England’ is ambitious, but often overloaded by the sheer number of events since 2016...A frustrating evening, then – like seeing your team put in a solid defensive performance but fail to get any shots on target. But, of course, we still believe.”

criticReviews.author: Alistair Smith
criticReviews.excerpt: “Dear England falls short of some of Graham’s greatest works because it never quite nails its wider analogy about what Southgate’s achievements might mean beyond football; nor does it offer much insight into Southgate, beyond what is already available in the public domain...This might not be quite Total Football, but, just as Southgate said he wanted to do with the England team, the play will put a smile on your face.”

criticReviews.author: Ben Dowell
criticReviews.excerpt: "still poignant with a perfect new Gareth Southgate"

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "The marvelous young actor Ben Platt is giving a performance that’s not likely to be bettered on Broadway this season. What’s more, this gorgeous heartbreaker of a musical has grown in emotional potency during its journey to the big leagues...The musical finds endless nuances in the relationships among its characters...Under the superb direction of the veteran Michael Greif, the show has been subtly refined, its brasher comedy softened, and the performances have grown in delicacy."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Platt is giving one of the greatest leading male performances I’ve ever seen in a musical, and the thrillingly modern and moving 'Dear Evan Hansen' is worthy of it...The musical benefits mightily from Greif’s dynamic direction, Korins’s vivid set design, Nigrini's cascading projections and an excellent cast...Benj Pasek and Justin Paul’s score brims with tuneful and thoughtful songs...And Levenson’s book is unfailingly smart...'Dear Evan Hansen' must be seen to be believed."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "So fine in its craft and rich in its gathering of themes that it rewards being seen again—and again...Platt imbues the character with so much pathos and lively detail that he succeeds as the story’s engine despite being almost pathologically passive...That Levenson has been able to find spots for humor at all in this grippingly sad story, and that Pasek and Paul have been able to turn those opportunities into songs of comic relief is a sign of the size of the ideas in play."

criticReviews.author: Terry Teachout
criticReviews.excerpt: "It’s smartly crafted, emotionally open-hearted and ideally cast. What’s more, it’s pitched to and has been embraced by millennials...yet its appeal is universal...Michael Greif has staged 'Dear Evan Hansen' with fluid, fast-moving simplicity...The score is not quite as strong as Steven Levenson’s ingenious book...Still, the songs work on their own terms, and the book is strong enough that it could be done on its own as a play...The best musical to open on Broadway since 'Hamilton.'"

criticReviews.author: Jeremy Gerard
criticReviews.excerpt: "The score by Pasek and Paul is packed with engaging tunes and insightful lyrics. The book by Levenson portrays teen angst taken beyond the normal boundaries with compelling dignity...Platt plays the title role in a movingly sensitive, career-making performance...Platt seems more to inhabit Evan than to merely portray him...The score soars, bringing us along with it. 'Dear Evan Hansen' is an intimate show with a gigantic heart."

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: "Platt nails each shifting mood and tone as a socially inept outcast. Original and up-to-the-minute, the musical has a lot to say—about parents and children, social media, and more...Stirring ballads and rousing group songs in the vibrant, varied score by Benj Pasek and Justin Paul ooze emotions. Director Michael Greif excels at guiding actors through complex stories—and his work has never been better...The show's so satisfying it deserves a thank-you note."

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "Not since 'Next to Normal' has a score tapped so deeply into the troubled psyche of its needy protagonist...The lyrics go beyond the spoken thought and reach for the unspoken feelings hiding behind the words. Better yet, there’s not a hint of sentimentality...Under the thoughtful direction of Greif, Platt goes beyond physical specificity to get under Evan’s skin and into his unsettled mind.  And the introspective, gentle score becomes the language of his troubled thoughts and yearnings."

criticReviews.author: David Rooney
criticReviews.excerpt: "What's perhaps most distinctive about Pasek and Paul's melodic emo-pop score is how beautifully it captures the peaks and valleys of adolescence, in the thoughtful lyrics and in the music itself...Playwright Steven Levenson matches the musical components beat for beat in his terrific book, which sets up with persuasive conviction what could easily have been a contrived premise...Across the board, the ensemble is superb, each of them registering rich moments of emotional complexity."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: “The chance to see two theatrical masterminds go at it for a few hours is sufficient justification for the effort.”

criticReviews.author: Austin Fimmano
criticReviews.excerpt: "There is love and fandom in every element of this show, like recreations of the movie's outfits and iconic lines"

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: “Having popped its cork early, the show keeps the bubbles flowing freely for the next two hours.”

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: “...hard to dislike and ultimately—as a medical examiner might say of these women—without a heartbeat.”

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "Megan Hilty and Jennifer Simard give boisterously funny performances as preening rivals"

criticReviews.author: Frank Rizzo
criticReviews.excerpt: “The storyline is cleaner, the characters are clearer, and the pace and the laughs are now non-stop.”

criticReviews.author: Johnny Oleksinski
criticReviews.excerpt: “Even if the musical doesn’t have a discernible heartbeat, Hilty and Simard ensure Death Becomes Her stays fun and fabulous.”

criticReviews.author: Dalton Ross
criticReviews.excerpt: “It’s a mission that succeeds more often than not.”

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "The latest Broadway revival, which opened on Sunday at the Hudson Theater, goes wider, a notably rich and mostly successful approach."

criticReviews.author: Gillian Russo
criticReviews.excerpt: "Even after nearly three and a half hours of 'Death of a Salesman,' I'd gladly stay longer to watch that story continue."

criticReviews.author: Rob Weinert-Kendt
criticReviews.excerpt: It is not only the casting of the striving Lomans as a Black family that makes this Salesman a departure. It is also that the director, Miranda Cromwell, has rendered much of the play as a dissonant fever dream."

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "Ms. Cromwell’s production is, nonetheless, emotionally wrenching as it digs fiercely into the heart of the play."

criticReviews.author: Greg Evans
criticReviews.excerpt: "The script is unchanged – and surprisingly accommodating to the fresh point of view...infusing the production with a legacy and identity all its own."

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: "Truly, it’s a rich and moving star performance and the reason to see the show."

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "There’s no doubt that casting a Black actor as Willy Loman (for the first time on Broadway, no less) adds a deeper dimension to this monumental role."

criticReviews.author: Peter Marks
criticReviews.excerpt: "The mournful irony Miller built into 'Death of a Salesman' is especially potent now, when our world so often feels as if it’s hanging by a thread. "

criticReviews.author: Joshua Barone
criticReviews.excerpt: CRITIC’S PICK: “ ‘Der Rosenkavalier’ is an ensemble opera in which it can be difficult to call anyone a protagonist, but Davidsen’s Marschallin leaves the stage the most evolved.”

criticReviews.author: David Wright
criticReviews.excerpt: “It’s great spectacle, but weak drama. And without dramatic credibility, ‘Rosenkavalier’ is reduced to its best bits, a song cycle in costume.”

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: "tries to engage the audience in unusual ways. But the execution worked better in previous productions"

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: "tries to engage the audience in unusual ways. But the execution worked better in previous productions"

criticReviews.author: Zachary Woolfe
criticReviews.excerpt: CRITIC'S PICK! "Ivo van Hove’s work is smooth, flexible and agile enough to walk the tightrope of any successful “Don Giovanni”: not stinting on the work’s darkness, depth and strangeness, on one hand — and, on the other, not snuffing out its wit, even silliness."

criticReviews.author: Heidi Waleson
criticReviews.excerpt: "Mr. Van Hove’s detailed, intentional directing made the characters and their motivations and interactions leap to the fore. 'Don Giovanni' can feel like a string of unconnected solo turns."

criticReviews.author: Mason Pilevsky
criticReviews.excerpt: A production with promise that would shine more fully with a full creative team.

criticReviews.author: George Grella
criticReviews.excerpt: "Van Hove, a marquee theater director...while his staging supported the form of Don Giovanni, it also stumbled too often in essential places, leaving the music-making alone to carry the success of this performance."

criticReviews.author: David Salazar
criticReviews.excerpt: "Van Hove’s production is not only worth one experience, but multiple to continue discovering the layers and colors of this most fascinating of operas."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "Like procedurals, it withholds information to maintain suspense"

criticReviews.author: Gillian Russo
criticReviews.excerpt: "Those sensitive to issues of sexual and child abuse may have some difficulty with Doubt."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: " 'Doubt' is an odd kind of mystery, less a whodunit than a wasitdunatall."

criticReviews.author: Sara Holdren
criticReviews.excerpt: "...Doubt is still a sharp and sturdy piece of writing."

criticReviews.author: Vinson Cunningham
criticReviews.excerpt: "At its best, 'Doubt' is about formality."

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "...Ryan and Schreiber, presents the play without any intentional new slant on its ideas"

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: "...a timely and now seemingly timeless piece of art that shed light"

criticReviews.author: Aramide Tinubu
criticReviews.excerpt: "Liev Schreiber’s performance cuts through a somber and confining single act"

criticReviews.author: Olivia Rook
criticReviews.excerpt: "...it appears that the blood really has been drained from this production, leaving everything in colourless tones and cast in Nick Schlieper’s sickly white light."

criticReviews.author: Nick Curtis
criticReviews.excerpt: “From defying gravity to defying mortality – Cynthia Erivo gives an extraordinary, shape shifting performance.”

criticReviews.author: Arifa Akbar
criticReviews.excerpt: "Erivo gives us a tantalising taste of her singing voice towards the end...It’s sad that the production plays so little to Erivo’s strengths, which might better have been reconceived as Dracula the Musical."

criticReviews.author: Dominic Cavendish
criticReviews.excerpt: "This radical adaptation of Bram Stoker’s 1897 vampire classic is a tour de force"

criticReviews.author: Clive Davis
criticReviews.excerpt: “Watching Cynthia Erivo in this solo rendition of Bram Stoker’s novel is akin to seeing an ice skater going for gold in the Winter Olympics.”

criticReviews.author: Sarah Crompton
criticReviews.excerpt: "It’s slick, soulless and all about appearances. There’s no jeopardy or really any true drama. "

criticReviews.author: Alice Saville
criticReviews.excerpt: “Alas, this time it feels effortful rather than fluent – and Erivo seems too stressed to offer more than the odd glimpse of Dracula’s coolly gothic allure.”

criticReviews.author: Sam Marlowe
criticReviews.excerpt: “I wouldn’t go so far as to say it sucks, but it certainly doesn’t bite.”

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "For all its harrowing power, 'Eclipsed,' shines with a compassion that makes us see beyond the suffering to the indomitable humanity of its characters. And although the events it depicts happened more than a decade ago, the play resonates powerfully today...Ms. Gurira’s play, directed with clarity and force by Liesl Tommy, reminds us of something profoundly important, and perhaps too easily forgotten amid our own country’s continuing racial troubles: African lives matter."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "In its Broadway incarnation, these women remain powerfully specific, and their relationships have warmth and texture...'Eclipsed' is consistently insightful about the ways in which the oppressed become inured to or reliant upon their oppression, even to the point of reproducing it; motherhood, biological or situational, is another of the play's major themes, and its exploration goes in surprising directions...It may be hard to watch at times, but you leave with your eyes wider open."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "A moving and must-see production...What’s most noticeably different is happening right at the center of the show: Nyong’o has managed to burrow further into her portrayal of the Girl...Her star power is not to be ignored. It doesn’t just make a production like this possible; it makes it legible, to the back of the theater and, more importantly, to the back of our souls. It asks, on behalf of women like this, a world away, 'Shouldn’t you know me?'”

criticReviews.author: Terry Teachout
criticReviews.excerpt: "Liesl Tommy’s production has lost nothing by being moved to a larger house. The play remains a staggeringly potent, perfectly performed snapshot of five African women who are fighting for their lives amid the roiling chaos of an unimaginably bloody war of all against all. 'Eclipsed' feels less like a play than a fictionalized documentary—but one of genius, a deceptively bald piece of storytelling...This is great theater. I doubt you’ll see anything more exciting on Broadway this season."

criticReviews.author: Jeremy Gerard
criticReviews.excerpt: "'Eclipsed' is a major achievement—a scorching work about women and war whose humor burnishes rather than undermines its seriousness of purpose. It features ferociously committed ensemble performances staged with power and finesse by Liesl Tommy...'Eclipsed' offers resolution but no hope...We can do little more than bear witness—something this miraculous play helps boldly to accomplish."

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: "Liesl Tommy’s taut staging provides an excellent showcase for the play. The cast is uniformly very good and while performances have deepened and feel more lived-in uptown, there are still few moments—light and serious—when individuals tilt toward being overly showy, as though they’re performing. Despite that, the play is unsettling and eye-opening."

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "One wondered whether that connection would be broken when the show moved to a much larger Broadway theater. Not to worry...The show hits the sweet spot for the serious New York theater crowd — the ideal audience for this intense drama — that often feels overlooked and underserved on Broadway...Playwright Danai Gurira delivers politics with passion in this searing drama...Superbly directed by Liesl Tommy and powerfully acted by a strong ensemble."

criticReviews.author: Elisabeth Vincentelli
criticReviews.excerpt: "As intense as the show is, it’s also leavened by raucous humor — a running joke about Bill Clinton keeps getting better and better. In the end, hope wins out over despair. If this is what happens when Broadway tells the stories of women, we can only wish for more."

criticReviews.author: Helen Shaw
criticReviews.excerpt: "As you watch Ectoplasm, you can hear noise from the outdoor dining up and down the block, even music from the clubs nearby. Its carpet unrolls damply in front of you as you walk in from MacDougal Street, a stubborn revenant of the pre-wealth neighborhood. It’s not gorgeous, but there’s tenacity ground into every red velvet seat. (In other words, I love it.)"

criticReviews.author: Victor Gluck
criticReviews.excerpt: Ectoplasm counts among its themes and topics: poetry, women’s rights, prostitution, women’s suffrage, love, death, the paranormal, the supernatural, fraudulent mediums – and the love that dare not speak its name, except here it is openly discussed, circa 1912. Each and every character has an agenda which is too many plot devices, while the actual plot never quite resolves itself. While the play has been given an elegant physical production, the script does not entirely hang together or feel satisfying.

criticReviews.author: Laura Collins-Hughes
criticReviews.excerpt: "Grey Henson...has gotten Buddy delightfully, entirely right"

criticReviews.author: Caroline Cao
criticReviews.excerpt: "have a holly jolly time on Broadway"

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "...this show is really elfin’ good."

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: "If there are occasional glimmers that Elf has more going on than meets the eye"

criticReviews.author: Meg Masseron
criticReviews.excerpt: "made this jaded critic believe in Santa Claus again for one glimmering...theater magic"

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: “The people at the Marquis Theatre are giving us the gift of professionalism.”

criticReviews.author: Howard Miller
criticReviews.excerpt: "The story it tells is a simple one, delivering a message of good cheer."

criticReviews.author: Joseph Pisano
criticReviews.excerpt: " 'Elf the Musical' will likely please the fans of its cinematic predecessor."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "In hewing narrowly to these questions, the production, directed with exceptional sensitivity by Knud Adams, creates more drama than its ingredients and its lifeboat of neatly differentiated characters would seem to permit."

criticReviews.author: Allison Considine
criticReviews.excerpt: "In any language, English is a triumph: Sanaz Toossi's Pulitzer Prize-winning play is a compelling exploration of how language shapes who we are and how we navigate the world."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Toossi’s engrossing game of show and tell takes us inside a foreign culture about which many Americans (including me) are woefully underinformed."

criticReviews.author: Sara Holdren
criticReviews.excerpt: "...sensitive, funny, and intimate, powered by its own craft and its excellent ensemble"

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "...the performances still have the bloom of freshness and discovery"

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: “The strikingly thoughtful and moving new Broadway play… looks at multilingualism from a different angle.”

criticReviews.author: Christian Lewis
criticReviews.excerpt: "Undeniably one of the best plays of the decade, it is both thought-provoking and deeply affecting. This Broadway run will thankfully allow even more audiences to enroll in Toossi’s class."

criticReviews.author: David Cote
criticReviews.excerpt: "Easily one of the most cohesive ensembles I’ve seen in years, the performers make little acts of kindness or meanness resonate loud and clear."

criticReviews.author: Jose Solis
criticReviews.excerpt: “Bradley and Greta share the galaxy of ‘Entangled’, an adventurous play by Simpson and Dean...Their distinct voices are what propel ‘Entangled’ from a traditional tear-jerker into a work of delicate rage...While Dean’s writing is overly restrained...Simpson presents Greta as a figure of unbearable grief and rightful wrath...Heaney’s unobtrusive direction allows us to observe, rather than react, as we wait for the two styles to collide.”

criticReviews.author: Darryl Reilly
criticReviews.excerpt: “Culturally relevant, emotionally resonant but languidly conceived, ‘Entangled’ dramatizes the issue of gun violence in the contemporary US...The play’s chief flaw is their overly literate dialogue...The preponderance of this self-conscious style is instantly wearying and makes the first hour an endurance test, undercutting the inherent poignancy.  The last 30 minutes are quite powerful with its climactic revelations and simple descriptions.”

criticReviews.author: Brooke Viegut
criticReviews.excerpt: “While artists have been creating...theatre about mass shootings...few are as poignant as ‘Entangled.’ It’s rare to find a play that approaches the subject with the candor, vulnerability, distress, and complexity this issue requires...A seamless piece that features many complex sides with tact...It's a masterclass in both performance and playwriting. Though the direction lacks some tension, Lorrain and Kautz carry more than enough grief and guilt within themselves to push the play forward.”

criticReviews.author: Janice C. Simpson
criticReviews.excerpt: “A truly moving meditation on grief and guilt...Directed with elegant simplicity by Kate Moore Heaney, the story is told in a series of interlocking monologues...Simpson wrote the dialog for the mother Greta...While Dean created the speeches for Bradley...This is far from the first show to confront mass shootings but it’s one of the most effective —and least exploitive—of the dozen or so I’ve seen over the last 10 years. And I wish there were time for more of you to see it.”

criticReviews.author: Jon Sobel
criticReviews.excerpt: "This epistolary two-hander...tackles an agonizing subject ripped bloodily from the headlines. In doing so it dispenses with dialogue and traditional dramaturgy, presenting instead two isolated characters in search of an elusive peace of mind...The story becomes more compelling as it gathers depth...To some degree, though, the production gets stuck in a web of artsiness...I think there’s more than we need here – lots of meat on the bones, but a little too much fat too."

criticReviews.author: Jacquelyn Claire
criticReviews.excerpt: “The playwrights take us deep into the minutest detail of the characters shattering. It’s like a theatrical version of a Knausgaard novel exposing us to the most honest, raw, microscopic view of humans in anguish. The writing is miraculous and shocking. They take you to the cliff edge and race your heart. You only wish that the storyline was some fantastical plotline...It is a work that should be seen in every conceivable space across the US...A brilliant staging of a complex work.”

criticReviews.author: Nick Curtis
criticReviews.excerpt: Peter Shaffer’s 1973 play gets a potent, almost expressionist revival by director Ned Bennett, which is better than it deserves.

criticReviews.author: Andrzej Lukowski
criticReviews.excerpt: An exhilarating and disturbing production that always stays true to the thrust of Shaffer’s play...

criticReviews.author: Dominic Cavendish
criticReviews.excerpt: My over-riding feeling is that I’ve not seen a more richly achieved production at Trafalgar Studios since its conversion from the Whitehall in 2004.  It’s perfect for that constricted main-stage, a boundless pleasure.

criticReviews.author: Sam Marlowe
criticReviews.excerpt: It’s a sweaty, sinewy, pulsing nightmare, a phantasmagoria of the dangers of repression and the potency of desire that grips and haunts the imagination.

criticReviews.author: Tom Birchenough
criticReviews.excerpt: Lean and hungry brilliance in Ned Bennett's production of Peter Shaffer.

criticReviews.author: Tim Bano
criticReviews.excerpt: Bennett takes this carefully structured, well-written play and tries to make it fit with a visual aesthetic to which it’s not naturally suited – the effect is stark and striking, and really quite brilliant.

criticReviews.author: Michael Billington
criticReviews.excerpt: Ned Bennett brilliantly directs the landmark 1973 play about a teenager who has blinded horses.

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "Awfully lowbrow…Dopey fun is one thing, but ‘Escape to Margaritaville,’ a paean to the pleasures of zipless debauchery, is pitched so low it will temporarily extinguish your IQ...A coherent aesthetic experience, in that laziness is not just its method but its message...The score is beautifully sung...It’s the songs themselves that are problematic. They may work well enough on the radio or in concert but, conscripted for theatrical service, grow quickly monotonous."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Hokey and sometimes pokey. But I’ll level with you: I had fun…The show doesn’t shoehorn Buffett’s songs into a story so much as cobble a story around them, extrapolating characters and situations from details in the lyrics, which is more successful in small ways than in large ones…Performed by a vocally overqualified cast…the score is pleasantly catchy…'Escape to Margaritaville' revels in its own goofiness. It’s not trying to be paradise; it’s fine with being a cheeseburger.”

criticReviews.author: Sara Holdren
criticReviews.excerpt: “‘Escape to Margaritaville’ is about as much fun as buying a dud hermit crab as a pet. It seems like it’ll be exotic, or at least cute, but it’s really kind of sad, and definitely a rip-off, and, at the end of the day, actually just an empty shell…‘Margaritaville’s’ best moments happen when director Christopher Ashley decides to take things just briefly into over-the-top weirdoland…The story sketched around Buffett’s big hits by Garcia and O’Malley has all the freshness of a rerun of ‘Friends.’”

criticReviews.author: Terry Teachout
criticReviews.excerpt: "One of the most mediocre musicals ever to come to my attention. The book is witless, the cast mostly bland, and while some of the songs are quite good, they’re all used in the most banal ways imaginable…Christopher Ashley has staged this sodden mess with the same lively energy with which he infused ‘Come From Away,’ and Kelly Devine’s dances and Walt Spangler’s sets are predictably excellent. If professionalism were all, ‘Escape to Margaritaville’ might be worth seeing.”

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: "May fit the bill if you’re in the mood for a breezy but dopey diversion…Shoehorning songs into a plot ‘Mamma Mia’-style doesn’t exactly accentuate Buffett tunes that already tell tales of their own. And the weak and weird book doesn’t help matters…A show one wishes was more fun. A saving grace is the cast, which makes the most of the material. Another is the batch of Buffett songs, easygoing ear candy — although hard-driving Broadway belts can work against the style.”

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "The hedonistic spirit of Buffett's feel-good 'gulf and western' music is on flamboyant display in this witless but colorful songbook musical custom-tailored for the fans...Garcia and O'Malley break no fresh ground with their corny story...But the placement of the Buffett songs isare smartly matched with the developments of the so-called plot...However well packaged, the show just isn't a good fit for New York...The production is ship-shape to travel...anywhere but here."

criticReviews.author: Frank Scheck
criticReviews.excerpt: “Even those unfamiliar with Buffett's songwriting oeuvre should find the proceedings relaxedly enjoyable…It's only when the writers attempt to provide literalism to the lyrics...that the show feels hopelessly strained…Nonetheless, the overall silliness goes down fairly easily, and even easier if you partake of the frozen margaritas...The show exudes an affable likability that's hard to entirely resist…It also helps immeasurably that such a talented cast of Broadway veterans has been assembled.”

criticReviews.author: Peter Marks
criticReviews.excerpt: "The lamely antiseptic musical...Insufferably dumb show, about a beach bum guitarist who falls for an environmental scientist...The musical is built around the Buffett song that practically everyone knows...The lyrics are used as such a literal guideline that one of the characters is actually 'nibblin' on spongecake' as the number begins...At the end...hundreds of beach balls are dumped on the audience...It was the only thing all afternoon in the Marquis Theatre that I didn't see coming."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "Spector’s hilarious poison-pen satire of educational wokeism has led us to that point with great care."

criticReviews.author: Gillian Russo
criticReviews.excerpt: "But as both the comedy and the severity of the debate increase, the characters deepen beyond caricatures"

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "A progressive school takes its mumps in Jonathan Spector's spiky comedy."

criticReviews.author: Sara Holdren
criticReviews.excerpt: “The show is a polite tiptoe along a cliff, a trek across a field of eggshells that as often as not are strewn atop landmines.”

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: "play seems mostly to be a plea that we get better at accepting that humans are imperfect"

criticReviews.author: Daniel D'Addario
criticReviews.excerpt: "'Eureka Day' is a cleverly staged social satire, one that earns enough goodwill"

criticReviews.author: Harry Haun
criticReviews.excerpt: "started out a serious drama and acquired a lot of humor along the way"

criticReviews.author: Naveen Kumar
criticReviews.excerpt: "...progressive politesse in shambles, profanity in all-caps, well-played emoji."

criticReviews.author: Holly O'Mahony
criticReviews.excerpt: "Both characters are wonderfully flawed creations, and it’s simultaneously moving and wryly funny watching them muddle their way through."

criticReviews.author: Nick Curtis
criticReviews.excerpt: "Diyan Zora’s stripped-back, well-acted production has the two circling each other on a turning revolve: but narratively, the play lopes off on all sorts of strange tangents."

criticReviews.author: Arifa Akbar
criticReviews.excerpt: "The play’s power, ultimately, lies in its liminal spaces: between dream, psychosis and reality, between fiction and its creation, and between the tragedy of death and the capacity for healing found within it."

criticReviews.author: Andrzej Lukowski
criticReviews.excerpt: "The big story here though is Kellyman, who has made a name for herself on screen as a supporting actor but could easily be a stage lead of substance if she chooses to go that way."

criticReviews.author: Dominic Cavendish
criticReviews.excerpt: "It’s a sensitive subject handled with finesse, acuity and surprising comedy"

criticReviews.author: Sarah Crompton
criticReviews.excerpt: "...a surprising and quietly powerful study of grief and families"

criticReviews.author: Sam Marlowe
criticReviews.excerpt: “If this is a wisp of a drama, these two actors give its gauzy translucency substance.”

criticReviews.author: Greg Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: “Evening All Afternoon may be a gentle play, but its emotional resonance is unmistakable.”

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: “Radcliffe is a spark plug, and his interactions with the audience are peppered with charming improvisation.”

criticReviews.author: Helen Shaw
criticReviews.excerpt: "And something more is happening here, too. Radcliffe makes himself extraordinarily available to us — his fondness for the audience radiates outward from wherever he is onstage."

criticReviews.author: Austin Fimmano
criticReviews.excerpt: “The participants' trust in Radcliffe makes for some impossibly tender moments.”

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: “ 'Every Brilliant Thing' makes for an unexpectedly buoyant evening of theater, but it never makes funny fodder of its dark subject matter"

criticReviews.author: Greg Evans
criticReviews.excerpt: "Every Brilliant Thing is unsparing and clear-eyed in its presentation of the realities of depression and suicide, yet glows with a hopeful, life-affirming aura that convincingly depicts the value of struggle, and the beauty in tenacity."

criticReviews.author: Aramide Tinubu
criticReviews.excerpt: "Radcliffe lends himself beautifully to the material, while simultaneously allowing the crowd to curate the experience for themselves."

criticReviews.author: Kenji Fujishima
criticReviews.excerpt: “Even Radcliffe’s seemingly effortless charisma can’t entirely disguise a shallow, generic feeling at the heart of Every Brilliant Thing.”

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: "Every Brilliant Thing centers on a list, compiled by the play's protagonist, of the details that make life worth living, and if Daniel Radcliffe isn't on it, that needs to be rectified immediately."

criticReviews.author: Matt Wolf
criticReviews.excerpt: "O’Riordan and her exceptional cast dig deeply into a psychic landscape"

criticReviews.author: Nick Curtis
criticReviews.excerpt: "riveting performances in a pitch-perfect revival"

criticReviews.author: Andrzej Lukowski
criticReviews.excerpt: "A play that will never be entirely mapped: O'Riordan's take feels pristine and ageless."

criticReviews.author: Dominic Cavendish
criticReviews.excerpt: "...it’s an unostentatiously stupendous production..."

criticReviews.author: Sarah Crompton
criticReviews.excerpt: "The play is written both naturalistically and with the nuance and meaning of a poem."

criticReviews.author: Dave Fargnoli
criticReviews.excerpt: “Profound expression of the raw wounds of grief”

criticReviews.author: Daz Gale
criticReviews.excerpt: "...'Faith Healer' is a gripping albeit at times confusing play."

criticReviews.author: Greg Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: ‘Feels fresh and revitalised’

criticReviews.author: Helen Hawkins
criticReviews.excerpt: "Director Rachel O'Riordan finds lighter moments in a tale of grief"

criticReviews.author: Mark Lawson
criticReviews.excerpt: "...emotional and narrative intensity, most resembles a spoken version of a Bach Passion."

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "There’s hardly a moment in the exhilarating, devastating revival of the musical 'Falsettos' that doesn’t approach, or even achieve, perfection...Directed by Mr. Lapine—whose work is so sharp it’s as if he were seeing the show with a new pair of eyes...Mr. Borle shines here as he has never before...'Falsettos' never feels like a singing time capsule. Its fundamental subject is that mysterious, maddening, uplifting, life-complicating emotion we refer to as love, which hasn’t changed in 25 years."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Few musicals have the range, idiosyncrasy and emotional punch of this profoundly unconventional and personal work...As enjoyable as the snaggletoothed and biting first half can be, it hardly prepares you for the extraordinary second...Finn pushes musical theater to the limits of what we can ask of it. Those who know the show may find fault with some of the revival’s choices...But flaws are written into 'Falsettos,' as is the impulse it elicits to forgive them."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "A heartbreaking revival...It’s hard to get through the last half hour intact...If this Lincoln Center Theater production, directed by Lapine, has any serious faults, they arise from that agenda. As written, Marvin is so nasty and erratic in the first act ...Christian Borle can’t resolve that contradiction and thus comes off a bit unsteady, at least until he regains his footing in the second act. The other principals, whose roles are more tightly written, are excellent throughout."

criticReviews.author: Hilton Als
criticReviews.excerpt: "One of the most dishonest musicals I have ever seen...What can you do with a show that opens with a song called 'Four Jews in a Room Bitching,' and uses AIDS to endow it with seriousness? The rot at the center of 'Falsettos' is slathered in self-congratulation. Finn and Lapine use Jews, AIDS, and so on to rope in a particular audience, which is then held captive to their seemingly endless array of self-referential songs and weak humor."

criticReviews.author: Terry Teachout
criticReviews.excerpt: "So how does 'Falsettos' hold up...Better than 'The Normal Heart,' but not nearly so well as 'Angels in America'. The first act, 'March of the Falsettos,' remains impressive. Notwithstanding Finn’s inability to write once-heard-never-forgotten tunes, the musical numbers are cleverly crafted and the overall tone is appropriately tart...In 'Falsettoland,' by contrast, a hideously painful situation is portrayed with a sincere but cloying sentimentality that occasionally curdles into kitsch."

criticReviews.author: Jeremy Gerard
criticReviews.excerpt: "It’s got tons of heart, unimpeachable performances...But while the production left me teary in all the right places, and laughing in all the other right places, it never actually took flight. It’s earthbound...What’s bafflingly wrong with the production has primarily to do with the visuals...That, combined with a first act that just works too damned hard to win us over, makes for some rough going...But then Act II happens and the show, for all its dark turns, suddenly seems light as air."

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: "Life is messy — as everybody knows...That includes creators William Finn and James Lapine. They don’t sugarcoat reality when it comes to love, sexuality and relationships...That clear-eyed take has always been — and still is — an intriguing strength of 'Falsettos'...Finn’s alternately lighthearted and poignant score in this mostly sung-through show is another major asset...Plan on being deeply touched and richly satisfied at this show."

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "This surprisingly fresh revival has been directed by original director Lapine, who plainly understands the bittersweet humor and provisional joy of that period...The warm performances of a terrific cast soften the underlying sadness of Finn’s breakthrough musical...The story is largely told through the easygoing score, a fusion of tuneful melodies with insightful lyrics...Borle’s neurotic hero is well matched with Rannells’ Whizzer."

It’s earthbound...What’s bafflingly wrong with the production has primarily to do with the visuals...That, combined with a first act that just works too damned hard to win us over, makes for some rough going...But then Act II happens and the show, for all its dark turns, suddenly seems light as air."

criticReviews.excerpt: "This surprisingly fresh revival has been directed by original director Lapine, who plainly understands the bittersweet humor and provisional joy of that period...The warm performances of a terrific cast soften the underlying sadness of Finn’s breakthrough musical...The story is largely told through the easygoing score, a fusion of tuneful melodies with insightful lyrics...Borle’s neurotic hero is well matched with Rannells’ Whizzer."

criticReviews.author: Ben Brantley
criticReviews.excerpt: "Strangely enchanting...The language of the script doesn’t always flow melodically. But van Kampen has an illuminating appreciation not only for period music but also for the gap between artists and their art...Watching Rylance’s Philippe experience Farinelli’s voice, we hear what he hears. And an actor and a singer temporarily turn a night at the theater in an anxious city into an Eden beyond worldly care, all the more precious for its evanescence."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Davies’s singing provides most of the high notes in this otherwise workmanlike play. The nature of the central musical therapy is barely explored; instead, we get contrived court intrigue, low comedy, a rushed quasiromance, and an equally hasty coda, delivered in a steady march of flat-footed exposition...The pleasures of Dove’s production—the music, Rylance’s halting propulsion, the sumptuous sets and costumes—gleam to no purpose, real jewels glued to a trinket crown."

criticReviews.author: Sara Holdren
criticReviews.excerpt: "It actually feels like there’s a much more interesting play hiding inside this one...Crane is uniformly fretful throughout. Rylance doesn’t really get much of an arc either...When Rylance isn’t onstage or Davies isn’t singing, it’s serious looking-at-your-watch o’clock...Honestly, even Rylance doesn’t save all his scenes...We in the audience are being asked to have the same experience as the king: Just listen and let it wash over you as a sensory experience."

criticReviews.author: Terry Teachout
criticReviews.excerpt: "By all rights it ought not to work at all—yet 'Farinelli' still contrives to cast an odd spell on the viewer, and its best moments have a delicate beauty that will stay with you...Van Kampen’s Farinelli is an inscrutable stick figure, while her Philippe is a walking thesaurus of stage-madness clichés. Nor does her plot have any tension...Thanks to Davies’s singing and Dove’s staging, 'Farinelli' manages to circumvent its dramatic deficiencies and hold your attention—if you love music."

criticReviews.author: Jeremy Gerard
criticReviews.excerpt: "It’s the best play and the best production of the season so far...Yes, it has a beginner’s nicks – unnecessary use of anachronism, a sometimes heavy-handed symmetry. But in the end, it’s wildly entertaining in the moment, and resonant in the aftermath. It’s not only fun, it’s really about something...And then there’s Rylance...Meticulously off-handed, it’s funny and sad, a performance to be savored in a totally engaging little triumph of a show."

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: "Claire van Kampen’s fact-based but liberally embroidered drama isn’t so sensational...Still, the drama at the Belasco is a richly theatrical reminder of what art can do...Rylance is riveting as the bedeviled ruler, but his star turn still raised mixed feelings. At times he is deliciously daft and spontaneous, but he's also occasionally too stagy and calculating to ring true...The play’s poky first half meanders, but it gains momentum after the intermission."

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "There’s not much to Claire van Kampen’s simplistic script...But with a lead performance by Oscar and Tony winner Mark Rylance in full sail, it’s enough...In the context of the period setting, the anachronistic language is barbarically contemporary...That’s a pity, since director John Dove has taken such pains to re-create the heavily gilded style of the formal Baroque setting of this production."

criticReviews.author: David Rooney
criticReviews.excerpt: "If the play is structurally shaky and thematically a tad thin, Dove's exquisite staging yields compensatory rewards...This is a potentially fascinating story...But the drama becomes borderline inert...Once van Kampen has put Philippe and Farinelli together she doesn't really know what to do with them...The deteriorating mental health of a monarch here doesn't constitute a sustaining narrative arc, even if Rylance's commanding performance remains the center of attention."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: CRITIC’S PICK: “ Seeing ‘Fat Ham,’ even multiple times, thus remains a revelation and a balm. It does one of the most important things we ask of theater: to rehearse, as many times as necessary, better ways to be — instead of choosing not to.”

criticReviews.author: Allison Considine
criticReviews.excerpt: “Ijames takes Hamlet’s political and social themes and marinates them for a modern audience...’Fat Ham’ is less about seeking revenge and more about Juicy winning justice.”

criticReviews.author: Raven Snook
criticReviews.excerpt: “...’Fat Ham’ keeps you cackling so consistently that the play’s sudden acts of cruelty land like punches in the gut.”

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: “This isn’t a tragedy. In fact, it breaks open and becomes a comedy complete with a big dance sequence at the end...I’d be interested to see another version of ’Fat Ham’ that brings that bitterness out further, slices toward the confrontational bones underneath the comedy.”

criticReviews.author: Greg Evans
criticReviews.excerpt: “Excellently performed by the entire cast...Ijames’ play resolves on an exhilarating, life-affirming note. Or, to be more precise, notes, as in song, and dance, and enough good-time gender-bending disco sparkle to win over all but the grumpiest of spirits.”

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: “At no point does this play feel like anything other than a big-fun Broadway show: It’s a smart, fearless and often wildly entertaining 90 minutes, filled not just with radical ideas but with absurdist spectacle.”

criticReviews.author: Naveen Kumar
criticReviews.excerpt: “ 'Fat Ham' is a total gas — the funniest and most invigorating new show on Broadway...The playwright’s own prose is lean and precise, with a vibrance of rhythm and association that hardly needs any supplementing.”

criticReviews.author: Lovia Gyarkye
criticReviews.excerpt: "This version of 'Fat Ham' plays like a modern sitcom, although with more tragic undertones. The slapstick humor and expressive deliveries leave little room for boredom, which is a double-edged sword."

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "The superb new production certainly honors the show’s ebullience of spirit…But as directed by Bartlett Sher with his customary sensitivity, this multihued staging moves to a heart-stopping conclusion.…It’s just a musical, no? Yes, but what a musical. The score enters your bloodstream, indelibly, upon a single hearing...And Joseph Stein’s book miraculously blends borscht belt humor with a moving depiction of Tevye’s conflicted heart."

criticReviews.author: David Cote
criticReviews.excerpt: "Bartlett Sher’s magnificent, life-affirming revival…Rich ambivalence runs through much of Sher’s elegant and deeply satisfying staging…This revival is splendidly acted…Revelatory direction, eloquent visuals and that sublime klezmer-inflected score —what more do you need? A great Tevye, and Burstein is nothing short of a miracle, finding the modern mensch in Tevye, as well as the hard-nosed, belief-bound peasant."

criticReviews.author: Terry Teachout
criticReviews.excerpt: “This production, intelligent and imaginative though it is, falls short of the mark, and the reasons why it does so say something revealing about the appeal of the show itself...Such things ought to make us weep—and in this production, they don’t... mostly, I think, because Mr. Sher has throttled back the feelings too far. One feels distant from his 'Fiddler,' neatly framed as it is by the vaulting proscenium arch of the Broadway Theatre, which is too big for the show."

criticReviews.author: Jeremy Gerard
criticReviews.excerpt: "A well-meaning but only intermittently inspired production...Choreographer Schechter has replaced Robbins’ evocative physical lyricism with caricature...Too often I had the impression of lines being recited rather than felt, and of lyrics being presented, rather than sung...In making a blunt connection between the deported Jews of Anatevka and today’s global tragedy of exile and dislocation, Sher does himself and this indestructible show a disservice. We’re smarter than that."

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: "One of the great and most enduring Broadway musicals. The new revival does a fine job mining this rich vein of material…Performances are very good, as is the lively dancing choreographed by Hofesh Schechter that taps tradition and some contemporary moves. But the curious scenery often gets in the show’s way. It makes for a distracting, busy and slow-pokey production of a tightknit musical."

criticReviews.author: Frank Rizzo
criticReviews.excerpt: "Some may take exception to some of Sher’s tinkering with the template of the beloved title, but few will find fault in Burstein’s gentle, lovable man of faith…Other touches seem unfinished, unclear or labored…Registering strongest among the new perspectives are the new movements and dances…Most of the cast breathes natural air into the production — sometimes with idiosyncratic touches that pop, and a few that fall flat…But in the end it’s Burstein who carries the show."

criticReviews.author: David Rooney
criticReviews.excerpt: "Sher's staging mines every dramatic nuance and every ounce of character-based humor in Joseph Stein's indestructible book…The dancing is simply extraordinary…The revival owes much of its emotional heft to impeccable casting..The duality of humor and horror is essential to 'Fiddler,' and as in every other aspect, this superb production captures that balance with enormous soulfulness...The show also closes the Broadway year on a magnificent note."

criticReviews.author: Peter Marks
criticReviews.excerpt: "Sher has done himself — and audiences — a huge favor with his astute casting, particularly in the choice of Danny Burstein in the all-important role of Tevye…It’s a wryly, fully realized portrayal…Around this central pair orbit other excellent actors…'Fiddler' endures as a meticulously well-built musical… Sher’s production underlines the inherent strengths and adds to them, with some thrilling dances and a beautiful physical production."
